transcription.text: I can't leave the old corner.
All right, everyone, what I've got is a whole bunch of stuff.
I've taken up the most space on the table.
Sorry about that.
I have a vintage Tandy Electronics beach ball.
Who remembers that?
The look of horror on Dick's face over there.
And my Radio Shack t-shirt.
It's not original, but it's Radio Shack themed.
I've got an Intel 8085 system design kit.
The individual chips actually came in there, and you had to assemble the board.
So this is an assembled version.
I do have mint in box, but I didn't bring that one, unfortunately.
It's got a schematic, even.
Who remembers Tom Moffat?
Everyone, yeah.
Everyone remembers Tom Moffat.
I've got original Tom Moffat kits.
So the Pocket Packet, the Listening Post and the WESAT.
He's original kits.
I've got one of my first big published projects in Electronics Australia, February 1993,
the Digital Storage Oscilloscope Adapter.
Did anyone have one?
I never built it.
You never built it.
Okay.
But you bought it.
Okay.
Yeah.
Dick Smith and Electronics sold thousands of those, and I sold thousands of copies of software for that.
So that gave me my big start.
That's what gave me my name.
I turned up to a job interview once, and somebody went,
are you Dave Jones who writes the Electronics Australia articles?
Yep, that's me.
So this is before the Internet.
So that was a real big deal.
I've got a Dick Smith Funway book.
That's just a bonus.
I've got the update to that, my original kit for the Mark III of this Oscilloscope Adapter
that was published a couple of years later.
I've got my 40-channel logic analyzer project that was published in October 1996.
EEPROM programmer.
I didn't design it, but I sold software for it.
Thousands and thousands of copies of software to who built their own EEPROM programmer back in the day.
Yep, that was a big deal.
I've got, oh, it's hiding, an original 1970s vintage, early 70s, I think, 50-in-1 Tandy kit.
So, yeah, that's pretty groovy.
And then I've got the, this is my original one I had when I was a kid.
This is the 200-in-1 kit.
So that's what I got.
I started out with the 50, the 150, then the 200-in-1 kit.
So that's it.
It was a kit, and it came if you wanted a front-end receiver.
It's maybe a little confusing to some people,
but it fed into a 4.6-megacycle IF strip.
It was a fantastic unit.
It was very good for amateur radio use.
They used the same dial on the transmitter, which I have now, and I'm working on that project very slowly.
The receiver, it's gone, like, around the world.
What happened was, when I was a teenager, I acquired it,
and I acquired it as a unit.
It was already put together.
And just to tell you quickly that I didn't have my amateur license at this stage.
And it's a receiver.
So I was all right.
I was all right.
And I built transmitters and all kinds of stuff because I worked at Ferris Brothers.
I had all the appropriate parts to get at the time, and I had so much fun building everything.
So what happened was, I left to go to Canada, and I thought I'd be only for a couple of years.
And what happened was that the actual unit survived going up to Barara to my mate, Grant Barkley,
who was VK2AXB at the time, and he said, I'll look after it for you.
But I didn't stay there two years in Canada.
I was 23 1⁄2 years over there.
So when I came back in 1991, I came back in 1990,
but 1991, I decided to go up to Grant's place, and he said, I still have all your bits and pieces that you built.
So when I went up there, I retrieved the Geloso front end.
I can't believe I've still got it.
So I've had it on, but I haven't had it connected up to the IF strip.
So I've replaced parts, bits and pieces.
So I'm thrilled that I've still got it, and it still works.
And so thank you very much for understanding my problem with having loving Geloso,
which Russell has helped me enormously, and so many others.
You guys were just great the way you've helped me out with all the bits and pieces.
So thanks again.
I'll stand by.
So I've brought a few things along.
One is a Dick Smith electronics enthusiast catalogue from 1981, 1982.
I've brought that along.
I've also bought the best kit that I've ever built.
It's a Dick Smith masthead amplifier kit.
It's all complete here, but I haven't yet got round to manufacturing it, but maybe next week.
I might get some spare time.
But one kit I did build is, and I don't recall whether it was a Dick Smith kit or what,
but it came out of Electronics Australia in 1979.
It was a direct reading capacitance meter that I built at the time.
And it has proved very useful for the fact that, unlike modern-day instruments,
it's got an analog display on the front of it.
So that has proved, over the years, very, very useful for looking at variable capacitors
when you adjust them, rather than waiting for a digital capacitor meter for the display to scroll and then settle.
You can just change it and look at the movement.
And also, perhaps even more importantly, for some of those small trimmer capacitors,
I'm not too sure what happens to them.
You get tin whiskers, but they become intermittent over time.
And so with this analog display, you can move the capacitor, vary the capacitor,
and look at the analog display, and then you can see where it starts becoming erratic,
and then you know that they do have an issue.
So it's a very useful kit.
I've got a couple of things that are locally designed, manufactured, and American imports.
I'll start here.
This kit was designed and developed by Electronics Australia in September 68.
That's a Jim Rowe jobby.
Yep, sure is.
It is one of a series of three that came out from Electronics Australia.
Now, I was still in high school when this came out, and I think whilst I was in high school,
I had a part-time job with kit sets in D.Y.
And I was building their Playmaster 3 plus 3s and 10 plus 10s and various other things.
I bought the circuit board, which has got an RCS number on it,
and you could tell in those days the size of the print and the ease of construction.
So yeah, the board virtually occupies almost the entire body of it.
I purchased this at a garage sale, mainly for nostalgia reasons, because I had the board.
I never finished it because by the time I was old enough to afford the parts,
they'd stopped making the box and a few other bits.
So I got this bit.
Then when I saw the whole thing, I thought, you beauty, I'll take that home.
So yeah, it's early, but there again, it's Australian design, manufactured.
It was pretty swish stuff back then, everything nice, metal boxes and well presented.
I'm not sure what it would have cost to build then,
but whether I could afford to buy the parts from kit sets or radio dispatch
when we were doing TAFE at Ultimo, where we all used to go, and do it that way.
So yeah, that's a nice local one.
Now, when I was working for one employer in the mid-'70s,
they had a number of Heathkit products we were using.
We had a Heathkit power supply, VTVM, Decade box, various other things.
So I took a bit of a shine to Heathkit, basic, reliable.
So when I had the opportunity, I was off doing my chemotherapy stint,
I did some eBay time.
It kept me sane.
I bought a couple of things on eBay, a couple, I don't know, geez, hundreds.
But what I'm getting at with this is that like most of these kits that we build,
and you can see it in the Dick Smith kits and the others,
there's always a pretty comprehensive guide.
So unpacking tools, et cetera, et cetera, your fancy Heathkit soldering iron,
your Exalight screwdrivers.
Oh, they smelled great, didn't they?
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
And guess what?
Not one page of safety.
When you go to do anything these days, it's all safety,
and the last page is how to build it.
So, yeah, yeah, do not drink the battery acid.
So, yeah, a builder's guide, other such things.
And I have one here in an original box, and it hasn't been constructed,
like Tim, one of those weekend projects.
But, oh, I even got the PayPal receipt.
But you can see this is how comprehensive it was.
You had a return policy.
You ticked the box for the warranty, et cetera, et cetera.
These are all the good things that I would imagine inspired developers,
EA, ETI, Kit Set, Dick Smith, et cetera, et cetera,
to put together good packages for us to build.
And they were good, and I think most everything you built worked,
and we could do it.
So there we have a couple of nice Heath Kit products,
shall we say an early girl,
and then a later more refined model of a decade box.
Now, I've used these a lot.
They're great when generating a current source.
So that's my little plug on kits, a bit of local and a bit of imported.
Yeah, very, very comprehensive for somebody
with minimal or basic knowledge how to solder in those days
and build some stuff.
So that's my stuff.
Thanks.
My dad built me a crystal set when I was a kid.
He showed me how to check the headphones
using two pennies and a piece of brown paper between them
to make a cell, right?
So the headphones weren't working, and to cut a long story short,
it was one coil in the right-hand headset.
And so I had to break the wire
and then very, very carefully unwind this very fine wire
hanging over the back of a chair
and found the break and then scraped the wires very carefully
and twisted them together because I didn't have a soldering iron.
And then I reassembled the whole thing and joined it up
and so now the headset was working
and using the cat whisker, I found the live spot
on the piece of gelina that was held in the little cup
and I heard music for the first time, and that was a big thrill.
I wanted to buy a number 30 valve when I went to...
Dispatch?
Yeah, Dispatch.
Anyway, I went in there and it was full of older people
and I was just a kid and they didn't want to serve me
and eventually they sort of got around to it
and they charged me 10 bob for a number 30 valve
and almost threw me out of the place.
What a thrill when Dick Smith's stores appeared
and you could walk in there and be greeted by friendly people
and always helpful and always got the parts
and if they couldn't, they'd help you to get them.
So time moves on.
I got into the Playmasters stuff.
I was living in a back veranda down at Narrabeen
and I couldn't have loudspeakers
so I built headphone amplifiers
and I had a pair of Akai headphones,
a turntable with a ceramic cartridge.
One of the things I heard on the radio
was a bloke talking, having a conversation with somebody
and it was very loud, you know,
and I thought, I wonder who this is
and it turned out to be an amateur radio operator.
I didn't write his call down at the time
but I determined that that's what I wanted to do
so I went out and I got my licence in 1962 metres.
I didn't do the Morse code
because I was too busy studying for my degree.
Gone on from there and I built various things.
I built a lot of loudspeakers and radios.
I remember building the one set with Magic Eye tuning
and I put it in a very ugly box that I made
and we used that as our radio for years.
I built this, so there you go, this one is still in service.
Initially there was just the amplifier
and one connection for external, which was the turntable
and I've had to add other things, you know,
as they become available.
They're on the back here, labelled.
So I had to rewire them to do that
and I marked the front of the dial with pencil
but I never got around to inking it in.
So that's the story with this amplifier.
The stuff that came out of that series,
the Playmaster series, was always good
and always worth building and I enjoyed doing it.
I love building stuff.
I love repairing stuff.
What I've got to do is get down to just doing one thing at a time
instead of trying to do 25 things at a time, yeah.
So that's about it.
Thanks for listening.

I purchased this off-the-shelf 27 meg CB,
marked it as the Hornet.

the radio had to go back to Dixie

and I found a Dick Smith electronics store.

I find this nice little amplifier kit.

Turn the beam down towards, back towards Tenerife.
S9, two meters both ways.
No problem at all.
Really good signal.
We carried on.

It was the amplifier.
Yeah.

and eventually we got up towards the UK.

in the North Sea,
between UK and most of Europe,
there's some wet squares

So this is a replica.
It's not quite a period piece, unfortunately.
I'd love it to be.
But it's a replica of what's called the KIM-1,
which was the first demo board
for a company called MOS Electronics
that brought out the 6502 CPU.
And the 6502 CPU was used in all the greats.
It was the Apple II, the Commodore 64,
a bunch of the Ataris.
There's about 30 PCs there.
And MOS was actually started by a bunch of guys
that defected from Motorola
that were selling CPUs for about $150, $175 at the time.
And they went, we're going to start our own one.
We're going to sell them for $20.
And here's a copy of the original ad
from September 1975, where they say,
yeah, you can buy our one,
which has been compatible with the Motorola one, for $20.
Or we've got this other one for $25.
It's got an internal clock generator.
And they said, if you get clocks for less than $5,
buy the 6501 and give your purchasing agent a bonus.
So a month after that came out,
and this was the demo board to use it as a ready-made system,
or you could just buy the chip by itself,
Motorola dropped their price from $150 to $30.
So it really kick-started the start of the...
Pure coincidence.
Yeah, so it kick-started the computer revolution.
And at that trade show, I believe,
was a young Steve Wozniak that bought a pair of them
that he used in his apples.
They had them in a jar, didn't they?
They had them in a jar.
The top half of the jar was the legit ones,
and the bottom half was non-working factory seconds.
But they didn't let people know that
because they wanted them to think they had a full supply.
And the really amazing thing is
they weren't allowed to sell at the trade show.
They thought they would be able to,
and then it turned out that they had some rule against
selling at Wescon,
so they had to direct people to their hotel room.
And then, like, yep, no worries,
and then take the cash there,
and then you could use a photocopier
and copy the documentation yourself.
So it was like this incredibly dodgy
but incredibly open thing where you could get it.

it's got the seven-segment display there,
it allows you to save and load tape,

because it meant you could get the magazines
and all of the people sharing code
